title: Polarization of Light
short_intro: Polarization is the restriction of the vibration of electric field vectors of a transverse wave to a single plane. It provides direct, unambiguous evidence of the transverse nature of light waves.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic concepts of transverse nature, unpolarized versus linearly polarized light, Malus's Law, Brewster's Law, and polarization by reflection and simple refraction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Double refraction in uniaxial crystals, ordinary and extraordinary rays, Nicol prism, production and analysis of circularly and elliptically polarized light, optical activity, and specific rotation.

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Unpolarized and Polarized Light
bullets: Unpolarized light contains rapid, random changes in the orientation of the transverse electric field vector E with equal probability in all directions perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
Linearly polarized light possesses an electric field vector that oscillates along one fixed, specific straight line transverse to the propagation direction.
Natural light sources like the Sun or incandescent lamps emit unpolarized light due to independent atomic emissions with random phases.

concept_notes.heading: Polarization by Reflection and Brewster's Law
bullets: When unpolarized light is incident on a transparent dielectric surface at a specific angle called the polarizing angle or Brewster's angle (p), the reflected light is completely plane-polarized.
At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and the refracted (transmitted) ray are mutually perpendicular to each other.
Brewster's law states that the tangent of the polarizing angle equals the refractive index of the reflecting medium relative to the surrounding medium.

concept_notes.heading: Double Refraction (Birefringence) and Uniaxial Crystals
bullets: Anisotropic crystals like calcite and quartz split an unpolarized incident ray into two refracted rays: the Ordinary ray (O-ray) and the Extraordinary ray (E-ray).
The O-ray obeys ordinary Snell's law of refraction and travels with the same speed in all directions within the crystal.
The E-ray does not obey Snell's law, its velocity depends on the direction of propagation inside the crystal, and it has a variable refractive index.

concept_notes.heading: Production and Detection of Polarized Light
bullets: Polarizers act as optical filters that transmit only those electric field components parallel to their transmission axis.
Malus's Law governs the intensity of transmitted light when a plane-polarized beam passes through an analyzer.
Quarter-wave plates and half-wave plates introduce phase differences of pi/2 and pi respectively between O-rays and E-rays to manipulate polarization states.

derivations.title: Brewster's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Light incident from a rarer medium of refractive index n_1 onto a denser dielectric medium of refractive index n_2 at polarizing angle i_p.
steps: Write Snell's law at the interface: n_1 \sin(i_p) = n_2 \sin(r), where r is the angle of refraction.
Apply the condition that at Brewster's angle, the reflected ray and refracted ray are perpendicular: i_p + r = 90 degrees, which gives r = 90 degrees - i_p.
Substitute r into Snell's law: n_1 \sin(i_p) = n_2 \sin(90^circ - i_p) = n_2 \cos(i_p).
Rearrange to find the ratio of sine and cosine: \frac{\sin(i_p)}{\cos(i_p)} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}.

derivations.title: Malus's Law Derivation
derivations.conditions: Plane-polarized light of initial amplitude E_0 incident on an analyzer whose transmission axis makes an angle theta with the vibration direction of the incident light.
steps: Resolve the incident electric field amplitude E_0 into two rectangular components: E_0 \cos(\theta) parallel to the transmission axis and E_0 \sin(\theta) perpendicular to it.
The analyzer absorbs or blocks the perpendicular component E_0 \sin(\theta), transmitting only the parallel component E = E_0 \cos(\theta).
Recall that the intensity of a light wave is directly proportional to the square of its electric field amplitude: I \propto E^2 and I_0 \propto E_0^2.
Substitute the transmitted amplitude: I \propto (E_0 \cos(\theta))^2, leading directly to I = I_0 \cos^2(\theta).

formula_sheet.name: Brewster's Law
formula_sheet.variables: i_p = Brewster's polarizing angle, n_1 = refractive index of first medium, n_2 = refractive index of second medium
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for non-magnetic dielectric media where relative permeability is approximately unity

formula_sheet.name: Malus's Law
formula_sheet.variables: I = transmitted intensity, I_0 = initial intensity of polarized light, \theta = angle between polarizer and analyzer axes
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid for ideal linear polarizers and analyzers

formula_sheet.name: Degree of Polarization
formula_sheet.variables: I_max = maximum intensity transmitted by rotating analyzer, I_min = minimum intensity transmitted

formula_sheet.name: Phase Difference in Birefringence
formula_sheet.variables: \delta = phase difference, \lambda = wavelength in vacuum, n_o and n_e = ordinary and extraordinary refractive indices, t = thickness of crystal plate
formula_sheet.conditions: Uniaxial crystal cut parallel to optic axis

formula_sheet.name: Optical Rotation Specific Rotation
formula_sheet.variables: \theta = angle of rotation, l = length of path in decimeters, c = concentration in g/cm^3
formula_sheet.conditions: Optically active solutions at constant temperature and wavelength

formula_sheet.name: Intensity of Unpolarized Light Passing Single Polarizer
formula_sheet.variables: I_0 = initial unpolarized intensity, I = transmitted intensity

formula_sheet.name: Thickness of Quarter-Wave Plate
formula_sheet.variables: t = thickness, \lambda = wavelength, n_o - n_e = birefringence
formula_sheet.conditions: For negative or positive uniaxial crystals where phase shift is pi/2

formula_sheet.name: Condition for Perpendicular Reflected and Refracted Rays
formula_sheet.variables: i_p = angle of incidence (Brewster angle), r = angle of refraction

graphs_and_experiments.title: Malus's Law Verification Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of transmitted intensity I on the y-axis versus \theta (from 0 to 360 degrees) on the x-axis, showing a symmetric wave-like curve peaking at 0, 180, and 360 degrees with zeros at 90 and 270 degrees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the cosine-squared dependence of light intensity passing through crossed or parallel polarizers.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual MCQs asking for intensity values at specific angles like 45 degrees or 60 degrees.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization by Reflection Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Unpolarized ray incident on a glass slab at angle i_p, splitting into a reflected ray at angle i_p and a refracted ray at angle r, with angle between them marked as 90 degrees.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visually proves Brewster's law and the perpendicularity of reflected and refracted beams.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical problems calculating refractive index given the angle of incidence or vice versa.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Nicol Prism Construction and Action
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A calcite crystal cut diagonally and cemented with Canada balsam, showing total internal reflection of the O-ray and transmission of the E-ray.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how a Nicol prism acts as an efficient polarizer by eliminating the ordinary ray.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions identifying the cement used (Canada balsam) and its refractive index relative to O-ray and E-ray.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the polarizing angle for glass of refractive index 1.5.
Unpolarized light of intensity 32 W/m^2 passes through a polarizer. What is the intensity of the transmitted light?
solution_steps: A polarizer reduces unpolarized light intensity to half its initial value.

solved_numericals.question: Plane-polarized light passes through an analyzer whose axis is rotated by 60 degrees relative to the polarizer. What fraction of the initial polarized light intensity is transmitted?

assumptions_and_limitations: Polarizers are assumed to be ideal, absorbing 100% of the orthogonal component and transmitting 100% of the parallel component without internal absorption losses.
Dielectric media are assumed isotropic and non-magnetic for Brewster's law unless specified otherwise.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Sound waves can be polarized just like light waves.
common_misconceptions.correct: Sound waves are longitudinal and cannot be polarized.
common_misconceptions.why: Polarization requires transverse oscillations occurring perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Unpolarized light has no electric field oscillations.
common_misconceptions.correct: Unpolarized light has rapid, randomly fluctuating electric field oscillations in all transverse directions.
common_misconceptions.why: Zero polarization means absence of preferred orientation, not absence of electric fields.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays have the same intensity.
common_misconceptions.correct: At Brewster's angle, the reflected ray is completely polarized, but its intensity is generally much smaller than that of the refracted ray.
common_misconceptions.why: Reflectance and transmittance depend on Fresnel's equations, not on equal energy splitting.

quick_revision: Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave, proven conclusively by polarization.
Brewster's law: \tan(i_p) = n_2 / n_1; reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular.
Malus's law: Intensity varies as I = I_0 \cos^2(\theta).
Unpolarized light passing through a single ideal polarizer loses exactly half its intensity.
